grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: Está en la biblioteca. Va a la biblioteca. Sale de la biblioteca. Volvemos al patio.
grammar.note_en:
A place and a destination are different parts of an event. Ana y Rosa están en la calle means “Ana and Rosa are in the street”: en locates them. Voy a la biblioteca means “I am going to the library”: a introduces the destination of ir. The destination is where the person is heading; the sentence does not say that the person is already inside. Rosa sale de la biblioteca means “Rosa leaves the library”: de identifies the place she leaves. These are useful patterns for these verbs, not a rule that every verb of movement must always take a. Entrar can use en, as earlier readings have shown. Here salir de contrasts with ir a and with estar en.

A and the masculine singular article el contract to al: a + el patio becomes al patio, “to the courtyard”. Do not write a el patio as two words. De and el contract to del, as met before: del patio means “from the courtyard” in the journey, while the same del can mean “of the courtyard” in la sala del patio, “the courtyard’s room”. Context distinguishes origin from possession or association. There is no parallel contraction with la: a la biblioteca means “to the library”; de la biblioteca, “from the library”. Nor do a and de contract with ordinary personal names: a Rosa is “to Rosa” or personal a with Rosa, according to the verb; it is not al Rosa. In this chapter a library book stays the library’s property while its location changes. Ana vuelve al patio means “Ana returns to the courtyard”: her paper-search action demonstrates the contraction before the exercises.

Ir means “go”. Its present forms do not follow the regular -ir pattern of compartir. The reading supplies voy, “I go”; vas, “you go” to one familiar person; va, “he/she goes” or respectful singular “you go”; vamos, “we go”; van, “they go” or plural “you go”. These are present forms. In the library plan, Tú vas y buscas otro libro means “You go and look for another book”; ustedes van a la biblioteca means “you all go to the library”. This chapter uses ir a with a place. It does not introduce the separate future construction ir a followed by an infinitive.

Venir means “come”. It normally describes movement toward the speaker’s location, or going somewhere with the speaker. Narration can adopt a character’s viewpoint. A listener’s location alone does not automatically make venir appropriate. Luis viene a la silla de Rosa means “Luis comes to Rosa’s chair”; the narrative’s attention is at Rosa’s chair. In ¿Vienes a la puerta?, “Are you coming to the door?”, Ana invites Rosa to accompany her toward their meeting point. At the end Luis is at the patio entrance when he asks ¿Vienen de la biblioteca?, “Are you coming from the library?” Ana answers Venimos de la biblioteca, “We are coming from the library”. De still gives the origin, not the destination. Venir is not just a replacement for ir whenever a journey has two people. The location and viewpoint matter. The supplied forms are viene, vienes, venimos and vienen; no drill requires an unseen additional person form.

Direction words must be read with an orientation. On this fictional map the outward walk goes straight toward the white-house corner, left toward the blue-house corner, then right toward the library. Vamos recto means “We go straight”. A la derecha means “to/on the right”; a la izquierda, “to/on the left”. These refer to the travellers’ direction of travel in the route sentences. On the return walk their orientation is reversed, so the same corners require the opposite turns. In the separate statement En el mapa, la casa blanca está a la derecha de la casa azul, “On the map, the white house is to the right of the blue house”, the comparison is between two positions on the displayed page. It is not an instruction to make a right turn. A camino is a path or route; an esquina, a street corner; a mapa is a map. Mapa is masculine despite its final -a: el mapa.

Volver describes the person or thing returning: volvemos al patio means “we return to the courtyard”; vuelven a la biblioteca, “they return to the library”. Compare vuelvo, “I return”, and volvemos, “we return”: the stressed stem changes to vuelv- in the singular form but stays volv- in this nosotros form. Salir means “leave/go out”; Rosa sale de la biblioteca is “Rosa leaves the library”. This chapter needs only sale. Prestar means “lend”: the library’s person lends the book and Rosa receives it. Presto el libro is “I lend the book”; la biblioteca presta libros, “the library lends books”. This does not mean Rosa owns the book. Devolver means “return/give back” an object: devuelvo el libro means “I return the book”; usted devuelve el libro, “you return the book”; no devuelven el otro libro hoy, “they do not return the other book today”. The larger-print copy is due back on the fictional Saturday arrangement stated here; that is a story-specific arrangement, not a claim about real libraries’ rules. Rosa’s planned Saturday return is expressed in the present with a day phrase; no Spanish past or future tense has been introduced.

The reference examples translate as follows: están en la calle / voy a la biblioteca / sale de la biblioteca, “are in the street / I go to the library / leaves the library”; al patio / del patio / a la biblioteca / de la biblioteca, “to the courtyard / from the courtyard / to the library / from the library”; vamos recto / a la izquierda / a la derecha, “we go straight / to the left / to the right”; vuelvo y devuelvo el libro, “I return and give back the book”.
